Kant had a theory of how the world works: there is no objective reality that we see; instead, our brains are filters adding space and time to reality. The objective reality is called nomina, which we can never know directly. Our interactions with this nominal create phenomena—the things we perceive. 

Kant's conception of the world creates three questions: what is the nomina? Who gave us these filters? How do our minds work and who created them? Lastly, if each person sees the world through their own lens, how can we know that everyone sees the same world?

Hegel proposes a solution to these problems. He suggests that the spirit (nomen) creates the material world; we are just shells of this spirit. The concept of nomen is hard to translate, but it combines elements of ghost, geyser, and gist. Ghost refers to a parallel spiritual reality, geyser to an expanding force, and gist to the essence or core of things.

The real truth in the world is the gist, not what we see. With this theory, all three questions can be answered: the nomina (spiritual world) creates filters, ensuring everyone perceives the same world through these lenses. However, a new problem arises: where did the gist come from? This question leads us to Plato and Gnosticism.

According to Plato and Nosticism, in the beginning of the universe, there was a supreme god, the monad or the one, which works by breathing and vibrating divine power. Through this process, he creates diads, which are forces that then create different realities.
